plan.title: [framework-gap] observable-scope mints need one human approval per cohort, not one terminal command per story

narratives.Description: Today scope:record-observable-scope and scope:record-intent-constraint mint one record per brief, so a cohort of N UI or intent stories costs N typed mints on a real TTY. This story lets both verbs take several brief paths or a launch manifest, show the whole frozen set of records, ask for the typed mint once, and write exactly those records without ever overwriting an existing record. Records that match a brief added by the same activation PR may ride in that PR and keep it brief-land shaped. The docs say that the merge that lands a record is its real control.
narratives.Overview:
1. Cohort form. `scope:record-observable-scope` and `scope:record-intent-constraint` accept one or more brief paths, or `--manifest <path>` (the `swarm:launch` launch-manifest JSON; its `xbrief_path` entries). One path keeps today's behaviour byte for byte.
2. Frozen set before the prompt. The verb loads and validates every selected brief first, then prints each record it will write (plan id, record path, brief path, `changeKind`, `allowedChanges`, `mustPreserve` or the intent facts), then runs today's `refuseNonInteractiveMint` once, then writes exactly those records. With explicit paths, a named brief with no valid contract refuses the whole set before the prompt. With `--manifest`, briefs with no contract of that kind are listed as skipped. Two plan ids that sanitize to one file name refuse before the prompt. If a target's record file already exists, the verb compares its plan id, brief path, `changeKind` and contract digest with the record it would write: when they all match, the existing file is left untouched and listed as already recorded (stamp and timestamps are not compared, since each mint writes fresh ones); when any differs, or the file does not parse, the whole set refuses before the prompt, names each such target and says to change an approved record with the single-story form (`scope:record-observable-scope -- <brief>` or `scope:record-intent-constraint -- <brief>`).
3. Write. A cohort run writes only records whose files did not exist before the run. Each is written to a temporary file and renamed into place; on a failure the verb removes the records it newly created in this run, leaves every pre-existing file untouched, and exits nonzero. Each record carries `cohortDigest`: sha256 of the canonical sorted list of record kind, plan id, brief path, `changeKind` and full contract payload, plus the repository slug. It is bookkeeping that ties the records to one approval, not proof of a human.
4. Activation PR carry. One shared check, used by `isBriefLandShapedDiff` (and so by `pr-closing-keywords` and the `verify-ac` Path B activation exemption), admits `.deft/observable-scope/<f>.json` and `.deft/intent-constraint/<f>.json` in an activation PR only when the record parses, its `xbriefRelPath` names a nonremoved brief the same PR adds or changes, that brief's `plan.id` equals the record's `planId`, `<f>` is the sanitized plan id, and the record's `changeKind` and contract digest equal the brief's contract. Any unmatched or ambiguous record leaves the PR not brief-land shaped, exactly as today.
5. Honest claim. `OBSERVABLE_SCOPE_REMEDIATION`, both verbs' usage text and `content/commands.md` name the cohort form and the activation-PR carry, and state that CI cannot tell a mint from a file an agent wrote: the record's control is the merge that lands it (the wording of `packages/core/src/policy/one-pr-scope-proof.ts` 14-20).
6. Tests beside each changed file: one path unchanged; several paths and `--manifest` write N records after one prompt; a refused prompt writes nothing; a named brief without a contract refuses before the prompt; a sanitize collision refuses; an existing matching record is left byte-identical and listed; an existing record with a different contract, brief path or `changeKind`, or one that does not parse, refuses the whole set before the prompt with the single-story hint and writes nothing; with one pre-existing record A and new records B and C, a forced failure on C removes B and leaves A byte-identical; `cohortDigest` is stable across input order; the brief-land check admits a matching record and refuses a record for another brief, a record with no brief in the PR, a wrong file name and a contract mismatch.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `scope:record-observable-scope` and `scope:record-intent-constraint` accept several brief paths or `--manifest <launch-manifest>`, print every record they will write, ask for the typed mint once, and write exactly the printed records; a single path behaves as today.
- A refused or interrupted cohort mint writes no records; a failed write removes only the records that run newly created and leaves every pre-existing record byte-identical.
- A cohort mint never overwrites an existing record: a matching one is left untouched, and one that would change refuses the whole set before the prompt and names the single-story form.
- A named brief without a valid contract, or two plan ids that map to one file name, refuse before the prompt; with `--manifest`, briefs without a contract are listed as skipped.
- Each cohort record carries a `cohortDigest` over record kind, plan id, brief path, `changeKind`, full contract and repository slug.
- An activation PR that carries records stays brief-land shaped only when every record matches a brief the PR adds or changes (path, plan id, file name, `changeKind` and contract digest); otherwise it is not brief-land shaped, as today.
- The remediation text, both verbs' usage and `content/commands.md` name the cohort form and state that the record's control is the merge that lands it.
narratives.Constraint:
- Accepting a merge-base record marked `mintedVia: activation-pr` under `requireHumanMerge: true` as human approval (comment 7070824329, findings 1 and 3): the env override, a plain `gh pr merge`, shared credentials, later record-only PRs and policy flips each defeat it.
- A forge `merged_by` read in verify (comment 7070824329, answer 2): a network read and a refusal that do not prove a human.
- An agent-written draft that carries a human-accepted stamp kind, or a wider `isHumanApprovalStamp` (comment 7070824329, finding 4).
- A path-only brief-land allowance for record files (comment 7070824329, finding 5).
- A cohort id that only labels records, or a loop that prompts before the inputs are loaded (comment 7070824329, finding 6).
narratives.UserStory: As a Directive operator, I want one typed mint to cover the observable-scope or intent-constraint records of a whole cohort, so that I approve N stories with one prompt instead of N terminal commands.
narratives.ImplementationPlan: Add a shared runtime cohort engine (scope-record-cohort.ts) used by both record verbs when they get more than one brief path or --manifest: load and validate every brief, build every record, refuse the whole set before the prompt on a missing contract, a file-name collision, or an existing record that would change or does not parse, print the frozen set, run refuseNonInteractiveMint once, then publish each new record with an exclusive create and remove only this run's records on failure. Each cohort record carries cohortDigest. One path keeps today's code path. Add a shared brief-land record check in pr-closing-keywords used by isBriefLandShapedDiff, evaluatePathBActivationAdmit, the story-line product-shape test and the verify:ac Path B activation exemption. Update OBSERVABLE_SCOPE_REMEDIATION, both usage texts, content/commands.md and the two record docs. Targeted tests beside each changed file.

## In plain English

The problem is repeated terminal work: a human must mint each story’s approval separately, even when approving a whole cohort. Batching can remove that repetition. Replacing minting with an activation PR is more consequential: it needs a reliable way to distinguish human approval from an agent merging its own proposed permissions.

**R1 cannot bind as written. R2 is a useful batching change, but does not establish the promised human-only property by itself.** Today, an agent can write a plausible approval record directly. Its digest proves consistency, not human approval. Moving that record onto the merge base does not prove who approved it.

Answers to the seven Stop 1 questions:

1. **R1 does not prevent self-approval.** Restricting the `activation-pr` label to human-merge repositories leaves the other freely writable labels available. Merge overrides, ordinary `gh pr merge`, and later record-only edits also defeat the stated premise.
2. **A forge merge record proves an account performed a merge, not that a human approved the contract.** With shared credentials, `merged_by` cannot distinguish human from agent. Do not add a forge lookup solely for that inference: it adds network dependency and possible refusal without supplying the missing proof.
3. **Approval must bind the exact record revision when authorized.** A product PR’s current merge-base policy cannot establish historical approval. Turning the policy on must not legitimize old agent-written records; turning it off should have an explicit revocation rule rather than accidentally invalidating genuine earlier approval.
4. **A draft should not carry a human approval stamp.** Record its producer as an agent and its status as pending approval, separately from any eventual approval evidence. Do not invent an accepted human `kind` or guess the future merger.
5. **Widening brief-land shape is reasonable only with exact content association.** Matching filenames or `plan.id` alone is insufficient; match the record’s contract and brief path to the corresponding changed brief, and handle removals, renames and duplicate identities.
6. **One phrase can approve N records**, provided the human sees the complete frozen set before confirming and the writer publishes those same records. Bind the cohort digest to repository identity, record type, plan ID, canonical brief path and complete authorization payload. A shared ID alone is bookkeeping, not authentication.
7. **R1 adds a policy-dependent refusal; proving its claimed approval would require additional enforcement. R2 adds batch validation and publication failure cases, but needs no new forge read.** #5980 alone cannot repair R1’s plain-merge/shared-credential problem. Split batching from approval redesign. R2 may ship separately as reduced ceremony with an explicit statement that the existing record-authenticity gap remains; it must not claim to satisfy the stronger no-self-approval test.

## Summary
Observable-scope mint records can be created only one brief at a time, by a human typing a CLI command on a TTY. For a cohort of UI stories this is the most-complained-about step in the delivery loop.

## Context
In deftai/evolution, the Agent Desk cohorts have 9 to 11 stories that touch `.tsx` files. Each one needs `deft scope:record-observable-scope -- <xbrief-path> --actor <name> --confirm --minted-via in-harness-ask`, run by the operator in a terminal. The agent can name the exact command but must not run it, which is correct: agent and CI shells refuse it.

## Expected behavior
One human approval for a whole cohort. Two possible shapes:
- A `--cohort <epic-id>` or multi-path form that mints every listed UI story after a single confirmation.
- A host-native approval prompt (an in-harness ask that the operator clicks) that the runtime accepts as the human attestation, so the operator doesn't have to switch to a terminal.

## Actual behavior / gap
The operator has to open a terminal and type the command for every story, often with PATH workarounds when the global launcher is not on the PATH. In the operator's words, it is "super annoying".

## Session notes
The human-only property should stay. The ask is to keep it while cutting N terminal commands down to one approval.
